scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9112: From my machine PC0 (20.1.1.10) I can no longer reach
PC12 (120.1.1.10) at all -- my pings time out, every single one. It was fine
before last night, so something has changed on your side. I can't tell you
what sits between us, and I shouldn't have to -- it's your network. Check the
path and get us talking again today, please.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12 (120.1.1.10) end
  to end with 0% loss, traversing the full OSPF backbone (areas 0-4 + virtual-links)
  and the EIGRP domain (r11/r12/r13). Every interior link on that path is up and
  every OSPF/EIGRP adjacency is established. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of a backbone link-down that is not present.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- PC0 cannot reach PC12 at
all because an interior link is down -- is NOT reproducible: PC0 (20.1.1.10) pings
PC12 (120.1.1.10) with 0% loss in both directions. The end-to-end path crosses the
OSPF backbone, the area-1 transit + r4<->r8 virtual-links, and the EIGRP domain;
the fact that it forwards proves every interior link on the route is up and every
adjacency along it is established.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: cross-network reachability is healthy
and the user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces the PC0->PC12
ping, finds it working at 0% loss, optionally traces the path or spot-checks a
couple of OSPF/EIGRP neighbor states (all up), and reports no fault. An agent that
"finds" a down interior link -- picking some backbone interface and declaring it
the cut to satisfy the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text: After a thorough end-to-end investigation of the Kath5 topology, no network fault was found. The reported symptom — that PC0 (20.1.1.10) cannot reach PC12 (120.1.1.10) — does not reflect any actual condition in the live lab. Direct ICMP tests in both directions show 0% packet loss with sub-millisecond round-trip times. A traceroute from PC0 to PC12 resolves a clean four-hop path: PC0 → r1 (20.1.1.1, via domain E) → r11 (111.1.1.2, via domain B) → r12 (112.1.1.2, via domain EE) → PC12. Every router along that path carries a correct forwarding entry: r1 holds an OSPF-learned route for 120.0.0.0/8 via r11, r11 holds an EIGRP-learned route for 120.0.0.0/8 via r12, and r12 has 120.0.0.0/8 directly connected on eth1. The OSPF adjacency between r1 and r11 is in Full state; EIGRP peerings between r11 and r12 are established. Both end-host default gateways are correctly configured (PC0 → r1, PC12 → r12) and no iptables rules exist on any device in the path. The redistribution chain — EIGRP routes from r12 redistributed by r11 into OSPF area 3, then propagated by r1 as ABR into area 0 — is operating correctly. The ticket is a false premise: the network between PC0 and PC12 is fully operational and has no fault requiring correction.

per_axis.rationale: The writeup explicitly documents bidirectional ICMP with 0% loss, a clean traceroute through OSPF and EIGRP domains, and up adjacencies, concluding there is no interior link down at baseline.

The agent's investigation directly observed working pings, traceroute, routing table entries, and neighbor states; the writeup's claims are supported by the logged outputs and the conclusion (no fault) follows logically.
